title: Intrinsic motivation (artificial intelligence)
summary:
Intrinsically motivated artificial agents exhibit behaviour that resembles curiosity or exploration. Exploration in artificial intelligence and robotics has been extensively studied in reinforcement learning models, usually by encouraging the agent to explore as much of the environment as possible, to reduce uncertainty about the dynamics of the environment and how best to achieve its goals. Intrinsic motivation, in contrast, encourages the agent to first explore aspects of the environment that confer more information, to seek out novelty.

Extrinsic motivations are typically described in artificial intelligence as task-dependent or goal-directed. In contrast, intrinsic motivation in AI refers to the concept of designing artificial intelligence systems that are driven by an internal reward system, rather than relying solely on external rewards provided by the environment or a human operator. The study of intrinsic motivation in psychology and neuroscience began in the 1950s, with Berlyne proposing the pursuit of an optimal balance between novelty and familiarity in 1960, and Deci and Ryan identifying an intrinsic motivation based on competence and self-determination in the mid-1980s.

Intrinsically motivated (or curiosity-driven) learning is an emerging research topic in artificial intelligence and developmental robotics that aims to develop agents that can learn general skills or behaviours that can be deployed to improve performance in extrinsic tasks. In computational models, the core strategy involves augmenting extrinsic rewards with intrinsic ones to guide agent behavior in the absence of dense environmental feedback. The total reward function is typically formulated as r = re + beta * ri, where re represents the extrinsic reward, ri is the intrinsic reward, and beta is a tunable parameter.

A foundational contribution is Jurgen Schmidhuber's formal theory of creativity, developed in the 1990s, which posits that intrinsic motivation arises from the progress in compressing and predicting environmental data. Oudeyer and Kaplan have also made substantial contributions to the study of intrinsic motivation. Despite the success of deep learning in specific domains such as AlphaGo, the ability to generalise remains a fundamental challenge in artificial intelligence.
